newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Finance Minister Kolodko quit, premier says.
newsitem.headline: Polish Finance Minister Kolodko quit, premier says.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko has quit and his resignation will be accepted by the president on Tuesday, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told public radio.
Cimoszewicz said he had asked for Kolodko to be replaced, as deputy prime minister and finance minister, by President Aleksander Kwasniewski's economic adviser Marek Belka.
Cimoszewicz said Kolodko had offered his resignation some time ago, to return to academia after three years in office.
The president's office said in a statement Kwasniewski would accept the resignation at 11.00 a.m. (1000 GMT).
Cimoszewicz said Belka's appointment, also likely on Tuesday, would keep continuity in economic policy.

"This is a person who with his knowledge and economic ideas guarantees that current conceptions of the economy, so far as fast development and finding ways to fight inflation are concerned, will be continued," Cimoszewicz said.
"The personnel change in this post does not allow anything that would place a question mark on the fate of Polish economic reforms and our economic policy," he said.

Kolodko, a non-party economist who was finance minister since 1994 in successive governments of the ruling coalition between ex-communists and a smaller peasant party, is credited with maintaining fiscal discipline and continuing some of the market reforms begun by Solidarity-led governments after the 1989 fall of communism.
He also drew up the coalition's medium and longer-term plans, Strategy for Poland and Package 2000.

During this time Poland has seen economic growth of between five and seven percent of gross domestic product a year, although the country has failed to meet its targets for cutting inflation -- which was 18.5 percent in 1996.
His ministry's authority was reduced during a reform of central government begun late last year and there was strong speculation at the time that Kolodko would step down.
Last month he strongly opposed Peasant party calls to restore import duties on grain -- earlier lifted because of soaring prices -- arguing this would boost inflation.
When the government agreed to restore duties on livestock feed grains, Kolodko openly criticised the decision.

Economists including centrist opposition leader Leszek Balcerowicz, who as finance minister from 1989 to 1991 launched Poland's market reforms, praised the expertise of Belka, who has worked abroad including at the London School of Economics.

"I know Professor Marek Belka as a very good economist who knows the Western economy well, but I cannot say anything about his ability to make decisions in difficult matters such as economic policy," Balcerowicz told private Radio Zet.
Balcerowicz was scathing about Kolodko, saying: "He had much more success advertising himself than in economic policy."

Jacek Dzierwa, analyst from Salomon Brothers in London, said he expected that the stock market would not react strongly. "I don't think the market will react negatively but this will depend on how the new minister will be."

Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Poland's biggest commercial bank, Bank Handlowy SA, said he did not expect any major market reaction and the resignation was not expected to mark any changes in economic policy.
"There should be no changes on price levels on markets...and the zloty should remain stable," he told Reuters.
"Foreign investors will have to digest the news and may, perhaps wait with further investment decisions until things calm down again," Ladko added.
